column1: # .github/required-contexts.tsv
# The branch-protection required-status-check contexts for `main`, and the workflow
# job backing each one. Read by the `required-unfiltered` fence in security-scan.yml,
# which asserts that no workflow listed here can be skipped — because a skipped
# workflow's required context hangs Pending forever and deadlocks the PR.
# FORMAT (tab-separated, 3 fields):  <workflow file>  <job id>  <context name>
# The context name is the job's `name:` — that is the string branch protection
# matches on. Lines starting with `#` and blank lines are ignored.
# ⚠ WHAT THIS FILE IS NOT — read before trusting it.
#   ⚠ FIRST, A CATEGORY DISTINCTION THAT IS EASY TO OVER-READ. Required status
#   checks gate **the merge of a pull request**. A DIRECT PUSH to `main` never opens
#   a PR, so NO required context is ever evaluated against it. Every context listed
#   below could be green, required, and enforced, and not one of them would resist a
#   force-push by a single inch. What resists that is `allow_force_pushes: false` —
#   a branch-protection FIELD, not a check. On 2026-08-10 that field is what actually
#   stopped an accidental force-push at `main` (a `git checkout -B <branch>
#   origin/main` had set the branch's upstream to `origin/main`, so a subsequent bare
#   `git push --force-with-lease` targeted `main`). The contexts were irrelevant to
#   that outcome. Do not reason about push safety from this file's contents.
#   SECOND, THIS IS A MANIFEST, NOT A MIRROR. Nothing mechanically proves it matches
#   the actual branch-protection configuration: that read needs repo-ADMIN scope and
#   CI's `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot do it (`GET /repos/{o}/{r}/branches/main/protection`
#   404s for the token). So:
#     - An entry listed here that is NOT actually required → the fence over-enforces.
#       Harmless: it holds an unfiltered workflow unfiltered.
#     - A context actually required that is MISSING here → the fence under-enforces.
#       THAT is the live gap — but it is NOT uniformly silent, and the difference is
#       what you hunt for at re-verify (Sec, F-3 accuracy addition, 2026-08-10):
#         · unmanifested AND path-filtered → a VISIBLE DEADLOCK. PRs hang at
#           "Expected — waiting for status to be reported". Loud and self-announcing.
#         · unmanifested AND carrying a job-level `if:` → SILENTLY GREEN.
#       Only the second shape is the dangerous residual. Look for that one.
#   ⚠ THIRD — AND THIS IS THE SCOPING ERROR SEC CORRECTED (2026-08-10). The residual
#   above was originally scoped to "a required context absent from the manifest."
#   That was too narrow: it should have been scoped to BRANCH PROTECTION. Required
#   contexts are ONE of five fields that matter, and the four this manifest does not
#   cover are the ones that held on 2026-08-10. Flipping `allow_force_pushes` to true
#   would be noticed by NOTHING — not by CI, which structurally cannot see it, and
#   not by the human check, which until now did not look there. Hence the widened
#   command below.
#   The gap is accepted deliberately rather than closed with a PAT: a token with
#   admin scope in CI would put a production-reaching credential in the CI secret
#   store, which collides head-on with the secrets-manifest CI/production
#   non-overlap commitment that `secrets-nonoverlap` exists to enforce. Trading a
#   documented sync gap for a hole in the non-overlap posture is a bad trade.
#   (Considered and rejected 2026-08-10, DevOps → F/CTO; Sec: would have vetoed.)
#   THE COMPENSATING CONTROL IS A HUMAN STEP, AND IT IS NOT OPTIONAL. Whenever ANY
#   branch-protection field changes — not only the context list — update this file in
#   the same change. Verify with:
#     P=repos/richmosko/mosko-fintech/branches/main/protection
#     gh api $P --jq '.required_status_checks.contexts[]' | sort > /tmp/actual
#     grep -v '^#' .github/required-contexts.tsv | grep -v '^$' \
#       | cut -f3 | sort > /tmp/manifest
#     diff /tmp/actual /tmp/manifest && echo "CONTEXTS IN SYNC"
#     gh api $P --jq '{allow_force_pushes:.allow_force_pushes.enabled,
#                      allow_deletions:.allow_deletions.enabled,
#                      enforce_admins:.enforce_admins.enabled,
#                      required_pull_request_reviews:(.required_pull_request_reviews!=null),
#                      strict:.required_status_checks.strict}'
#   ⚠ CHECK THE SECOND COMMAND'S OUTPUT AGAINST THIS EXPECTED POSTURE — which is a
#   JUDGMENT THIS PROJECT OWNS, deliberately NOT a record of what the API currently
#   returns. A committed value is a claim that goes stale silently; that is the exact
#   defect this whole line of work has been removing. The VALUES are derivable by
#   running the command. The EXPECTATION is the thing worth writing down:
#     · allow_force_pushes                → expected FALSE. History on `main` is not
#       rewritable. This is the field that stops the accident described above, and it
#       is the one no CI check can ever observe.
#     · allow_deletions                   → expected FALSE. `main` is not deletable.
#     · enforce_admins                    → expected TRUE. A rule the owner can walk
#       around is a rule that is off on the days it matters.
#     · required_pull_request_reviews     → expected PRESENT. Solo-maintainer, so the
#       approval COUNT may legitimately be 0; presence is what carries the review
#       plumbing (e.g. dismiss-stale behaviour) and is what to confirm.
#     · strict (require branches up to date) → expected TRUE. Without it a context can
#       pass against a base that no longer exists.
#   If an observed value disagrees with an expectation above, that is EITHER a
#   misconfiguration OR a deliberate change nobody recorded. Both need a human; do
#   not silently update the expectation to match what you observed — that converts a
#   finding into a rubber stamp.
#   Run this at every promotion. Do not assume this file is current because CI is
#   green: CI green says ONLY that what IS listed here is unfiltered.
# ⚠ PUSH SAFETY — the standing incantation, because a discipline fails exactly once.
#   `git checkout -B <branch> origin/main` sets the branch's upstream to `origin/main`,
#   so a later bare `git push --force-with-lease` TARGETS MAIN. The fix is not "remember
#   to fix the upstream afterwards" — a rule you must remember to apply is a rule that
#   gets skipped. Prefer the form that names its target and cannot silently inherit it:
#     git push --force-with-lease=<branch>:<sha> origin HEAD:<branch>
#   (Sec, 2026-08-10.) This belongs wherever the re-derive-don't-conflict-resolve
#   method is written down; it is restated here because this file is where the
#   force-push question gets asked.

# These were advisory until 2026-08-10 because a `paths:` filter made them
# un-requireable — a filtered workflow's required context hangs Pending forever.
# Dropping the filters is what made them eligible; keeping them dropped is what keeps

# The fence that enforces this file, listed in it deliberately. If
# `required-unfiltered` is not itself a required context, someone can break it and
# merge anyway — and the failure is quiet, because a broken guard looks exactly like
# a satisfied one. It is self-consistent to list: security-scan.yml carries no
# `paths:` filter and this job carries no `if:`, so it checks itself and passes.
# ⚠ Whether it is in branch protection at any given moment is NOT recorded here —
# that is a live fact, derivable by the command above, and a recorded copy of it
# would go stale silently. If it is ever NOT required, that is the thing to fix.
security-scan.yml
